mn2:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.
mn2:1.3: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:
mn2:2.1: ‘Bhikkhus, I shall expound to you a discourse on the restraint of all the taints (āsava),
mn2:2.2: listen and heed well what I shall say.’
mn2:3.1: ‘Bhikkhus. I say that there is an exhaustion of taints in one who knows and sees, not in one who does not know and see.
mn2:3.4: ‘When a man attends unwisely both unarisen taints arise and arisen taints increase.
mn2:3.5: When he attends wisely, both unarisen taints do not arise and arisen taints are abandoned.
mn2:5.1: ‘What taints can be abandoned by seeing?
mn2:5.2: ‘Here, bhikkhus, an untaught ordinary man, who has no regard for Noble Ones, and is inconversant with their Dhamma and undisciplined in it, who has no regard for True Men and is inconversant with their Dhamma and undisciplined in it,
mn2:5.3: does not understand what dhammas are fit for attention, or what dhammas are unfit for attention.
mn2:5.4: Since that is so, he does not attend to dhammas fit for attention and he attends to dhammas unfit for attention.
mn2:6.1: ‘What dhammas unfit for attention does he attend to?
mn2:6.2: They are dhammas such that when he attends to them with his attention, the unarisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance arise in him, or the arisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance increase in him.
mn2:6.5: These are the dhammas unfit for attention to which he attends.
mn2:6.6: And what dhammas fit for attention does not attend to?
mn2:6.7: They are dhammas such that when he attends to them with his attention, the unarisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance, do not arise in him, and the arisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance are abandoned in him.
mn2:6.8: the unarisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance, do not arise in him, and the arisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance are abandoned in him.
mn2:6.10: These are the dhammas fit for attention to which he does not attend.
mn2:7.1: By attending to dhammas unfit for attention and by not attending to dhammas fit for attention, both unarisen taints arise and arisen taints increase.
mn2:7.3: Was I in past time? Was I not in past time? What was I in past time? How was I in past time? Having been what, what was I in past time?
mn2:7.4: Shall I be in future time? Shall I not be in future time? What shall I be in future time? How shall I be in future time? Having been what, what shall I be in future time?”
mn2:7.5: Or else he is doubtful in himself about presently existing time thus: “
mn2:7.6: Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Whence will this being have come? Whither will it be bound?”’
mn2:8.1: ‘When he attends unwisely in this way, one of six kinds of view arises in him:
mn2:8.2: The view self exists for me arises in him as true and established,
mn2:8.3: or the view no self exists for me arises in him as true and established,
mn2:8.4: or the view I perceive self with self arises in him as true and established,
mn2:8.5: or the view I perceive not-self with self arises in him as true and established,
mn2:8.6: or the view I perceive self with not-self arises in him as true and established,
mn2:8.7: or else he has some such view as
mn2:8.8: It is this my self that speaks and feels, and that experiences here or there the ripening of good and bad actions; but this my self is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, and it will endure as long as eternity.
mn2:8.9: “This type of view is called the thicket of views, the wilderness of views, the contortion of views, the vacillation of views, the fetter of views.
mn2:8.10: No untaught ordinary man bound by the fetter of views is freed by birth, ageing and death, by sorrows and lamentations, by pains, griefs and despairs;
mn2:8.11: he is not freed from suffering, I say.
mn2:9.2: ‘The well-taught disciple of Noble Ones, who has regard for Noble Ones, and is conversant with their Dhamma and disciplined in it, who has regard for True Men and is conversant with their Dhamma and disciplined in it,
mn2:9.3: understands what dhammas are fit for attention and what dhammas are unfit for attention.
mn2:9.4: Since that is so, he does not attend to dhammas unfit for attention. He attends to dhammas fit for attention.
mn2:10.1: ‘What dhammas unfit for attention does he not attend to?
mn2:10.2: They are dhammas such that when he attends to them the unarisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance, arise in him, or the arisen taints of sensual pleasure, being and ignorance increase in him.
mn2:10.5: These are the dhammas unfit for attention that he does not attend to.
mn2:10.6: ‘And what dhammas fit for attention does he attend to?
mn2:10.7: They are dhammas such that when he attends to them the unarisen taints of sensual desire,
mn2:10.9: and ignorance, do not arise in him and the arisen taints of sensual desire, being and ignorance are abandoned in him.
mn2:10.10: These are the dhammas fit for attention that he attends to.
mn2:10.11: ‘By not attending to dhammas unfit for attention and by attending to dhammas fit for attention both unarisen taints do not arise and arisen taints are abandoned.
mn2:11.1: ‘This is how he attends wisely: this is suffering, and this is the origin of suffering and this is the cessation of suffering, and this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
mn2:11.2: ‘When he attends wisely in this way, three fetters are abandoned in him:
mn2:11.3: the embodiment-view, uncertainty, and adherence to rites and rituals.
mn2:11.4: ‘These are called the taints that can be abandoned by seeing.
mn2:12.1: ‘What taints can be abandoned by restraining?
mn2:12.2: Here a bhikkhu reflecting wisely abides with the eye faculty restrained.
mn2:12.3: While taints and fever of defilement might arise in a bhikkhu who abode with the eye faculty unrestrained, there are no taints or fever of defilement in him when he abides with the eye faculty restrained.
mn2:12.4: ‘Reflecting wisely he abides with the ear faculty restrained …
mn2:12.8: ‘Reflecting wisely he abides with the mind faculty restrained …
mn2:12.9: there are no taints or fever of defilement in him when he abides with the mind faculty restrained.
mn2:12.10: ‘While taints and fever of difilement might arise in one who abode unrestrained, there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who abides restrained.
mn2:12.11: ‘These are called the taints that can be abandoned by restraining.
mn2:13.1: ‘What taints can be abandoned by using?
mn2:13.2: ‘Here a bhikkhu reflecting wisely uses a robe
mn2:13.3: only for protection from cold, for protection from heat, for protection from contact with gadflies, flics, wind, burning and creeping things, and only for the purpose of concealing what disturbs conscience.
mn2:14.2: neither for amusement nor for intoxication (of vanity), nor for smartening, nor for embellishment, but only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the life divine (considering:) “Thus shall I terminate old feelings without arousing new feelings and blameless, shall live in comfort and health.”
mn2:15.1: ‘Reflecting wisely he uses a resting place
mn2:15.2: only for protection from cold, for protection from heat, for protection from gadflies, flies, wind, burning and creeping things, only for the purpose of warding off the perils of climate for enjoying retreat.
mn2:16.1: ‘Reflecting wisely he uses the requisite of medicine as cure for the sick,
mn2:17.1: ‘While taints and fever of defilement might arise in one who did not use (the requisites thus), there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who uses (them thus).
mn2:17.2: ‘These are called taints that can be abandoned by using.
mn2:18.1: ‘What taints can be abandoned by enduring?
mn2:18.2: ‘Here a bhikkhu reflecting wisely bears cold, heat, hunger, thirst and contact with gadflies, flies, wind, burning and creeping things, he endures ill-spoken, unwelcome words and arisen bodily feelings that are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, disagreeable, distressing and menacing to life.
mn2:18.3: ‘While taints and fever of defilement might arise in one who did not endure, there are no taints and fever of defilement in one who endures.
mn2:18.4: ‘These are called the taints that can be abandoned by enduring.
mn2:19.1: ‘What taints can be abandoned by avoiding?
mn2:19.2: ‘Here a bhikkhu reflecting wisely avoids a savage elephant, a savage horse, a savage bull, a savage dog, a snake, a stump, a bramble (patch), a chasm, a cliff, a cess-pit, a sewer;
mn2:19.3: reflecting wisely he avoids sitting on unsuitable seats, wandering to unsuitable resorts, frequenting bad friends, such that wise companions in the life divine might believe to be evidence of evil-doing.
mn2:19.4: ‘While taints and fever of defilement might arise in one who did not avoid (these things), there are no taints and fever of defilement in one who avoids (them).
mn2:19.5: ‘These are called taints that can be abandoned by avoiding.
mn2:20.1: ‘What taints can be abandoned by removing?
mn2:20.2: ‘Here a bhikkhu reflecting wisely does not endure an arisen thought affected by sensual desire … by ill-will … by cruelty; he abandons it, removes it, does away with and annihilates it. He does not endure arisen, evil, unprofitable dhammas; he abandons them, removes them, does away with and annihilates them.
mn2:20.3: ‘While taints and fever of defilement might arise in one who did not remove (these thoughts), there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who removes (them).
mn2:20.4: ‘These are called taints that can be abandoned by removing.
mn2:21.1: ‘What taints can be abandoned by developing?
mn2:21.2: ‘Here a bhikkhu reflecting wisely develops the mindfulness enlightenment-factor which has seclusion, passionlessness and cessation for its support and changes to relinquishment.
mn2:21.3: ‘He develops the investigation of Dhamma enlightenment-factor
mn2:21.8: ‘ … the equanimity enlightenment-factor, which has seclusion, passionlessness and cessation for its support and changes to relinquishment.
mn2:21.9: ‘While taints and fever of defilement might arise in one who did not develop (them), there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who develops (them).
mn2:21.10: ‘These are called taints that can be abandoned by developing.
mn2:22.1: ‘As soon as a bhikkhu’s taints that can be abandoned by seeing (insight) have been so abandoned, as his taints that can be abandoned by restraining have been so abandoned, as his taints that can be abandoned by using have been so abandoned, as his taints that can be abandoned by enduring have been so abandoned, as his taints that can be abandoned by avoiding have been so abandoned, as his taints that can be abandoned by removing have been so abandoned, as his taints that can be abandoned by developing have been so abandoned—
mn2:22.2: then he is called a bhikkhu who dwells restrained with the restraint of all the taints: he has severed craving, flung off the fetters, and has made an end of suffering with the complete penetration of conceit.’
mn2:22.3: That was what the Blessed One said.
mn2:22.4: The bhikkhus where satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
